title: “NO. NOT UNTIL YOU SUFFER LIKE I DID.” — CAN YOU WITHHOLD SEX TO PUNISH YOUR SPOUSE?
paragraphs:
“NO. NOT UNTIL YOU SUFFER LIKE I DID.” — CAN YOU WITHHOLD SEX TO PUNISH YOUR SPOUSE?
When the Marriage Bed Becomes a Battlefield, Scripture Asks a Question More Dangerous Than “Who Started It?”: Are You Still Loving Your Spouse Like Someone Jesus Died to Redeem?

Two people can lie inches apart beneath the same blanket while emotionally living in different countries. They can share a mortgage, children, meals, photographs, a church pew, even prayers before dinner...
and still use silence as a knife.
Maybe the argument happened hours ago.
Maybe it happened three years ago and never really ended.
And somewhere beneath the rejection is a sentence nobody says aloud:
Now you know how it feels.
That is where this conversation becomes uncomfortable.
Because there are legitimate reasons a husband or wife may not be ready or able to have sex.
Marital conflict can deeply affect emotional and physical intimacy.

And where there is abuse, intimidation, coercion, threats, or fear, the biblical response is never to pressure the endangered spouse into sexual activity. Sexual intimacy within Christian marriage is meant to express covenant love—not domination. No verse of Scripture should ever be twisted into permission to force, threaten, manipulate, or sexually coerce another human being.
So this article is not asking:
“Must a spouse say yes every time?”
The question is far more specific.
Can a Christian deliberately withhold sexual intimacy for the purpose of punishing, controlling, humiliating, manipulating, or getting revenge on a spouse?
And on that question, Scripture refuses to let us hide behind excuses.
Paul writes to married believers in Corinth:
Let the husband give his wife what is due within the marriage relationship, and likewise the wife to her husband.
Then Paul becomes even more direct:
Notice the words Paul did not use.
“Husbands, your wives owe you whatever you demand.”
That one word destroys a mountain of selfish interpretations.
Neither spouse is handed a biblical weapon.
Both are handed a biblical responsibility.
Paul continues by describing even temporary abstinence as something undertaken “ἐκ συμφώνου” — ek symphōnou — by mutual agreement, for a time, in connection with prayer, followed by reunion.
Not “You disappointed me, so now I control whether you feel loved.”
Not “I know exactly where you are vulnerable, and I am going to use that vulnerability against you.”
That is punishment wearing the clothes of intimacy.
And sometimes Christians become extremely creative at baptizing revenge.
We do not say, “I want to hurt you.”
We simply discover what matters most to our spouse...
Until the marriage becomes a courtroom where both spouses are simultaneously prosecutor, defendant, judge, and executioner.
But marriage was never designed to become a courtroom.
It was designed to become a covenant.
And covenant love does something our flesh hates.
It refuses to make revenge its god.
Maybe there was an argument and no apology.
Maybe you have been carrying responsibilities nobody notices.
Maybe every affectionate touch now feels suspicious because you think, You ignore me all day and suddenly remember I exist when you want sex.
That pain should not be mocked.
Because sometimes what looks like “withholding sex” from one side feels like “I cannot emotionally connect with someone who refuses to listen to me” from the other.
Those are not necessarily the same thing.
So before quoting 1 Corinthians 7 at your spouse, perhaps you should allow 1 Corinthians 7 to interrogate you.
Are you demanding intimacy while refusing tenderness?
Are you asking for your spouse’s body while neglecting your spouse’s heart?
Are you treating sex as an entitlement instead of a gift shared within covenant love?
Do you become angry when your spouse says no?
If so, you are not defending biblical marriage.
You are violating the spirit of Christlike love.
Because the Bible that says, “Do not deprive one another,” also tells husbands:
“Οἱ ἄνδρες, ἀγαπᾶτε τὰς γυναῖκας, καθὼς καὶ ὁ Χριστὸς ἠγάπησεν τὴν ἐκκλησίαν...”
“Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church...”
And how did Christ love His church?
He did not ask, “How much can I take?”
That is why Christian marital intimacy can never be reduced to:
“How can I protect what God has entrusted to us?”
“How can we heal what resentment has damaged?”
“How can we become one again instead of winning another argument?”
Peter tells husbands to live with their wives “κατὰ γνῶσιν” — kata gnōsin — according to knowledge, with understanding, giving honor, recognizing them as fellow heirs of the grace of life.
Those words belong in the bedroom too.
Imagine what would happen if Christian husbands stopped asking only, “Why doesn’t she want me?” and sometimes asked, “What is happening inside the woman I promised to cherish?”

Imagine what would happen if Christian wives stopped asking only, “How can I make him understand how angry I am?” and sometimes asked, “Am I using rejection specifically because I know it will hurt him?”
Imagine if both stopped keeping score.
Because that is where punishment begins.
You said something six years ago that I technically forgave but emotionally preserved in a glass case.
This is how marriages become cold without anybody filing for divorce.
The wedding photographs remain on the wall.
One more score added to the ledger.
Until two people who once could not wait to touch each other cannot remember how to talk without defending themselves.
Because Satan does not necessarily need to destroy every Christian marriage through adultery.
Sometimes years of unresolved rejection will do.
Sometimes the refusal to repent will do.
Sometimes two Christians can destroy intimacy while both remain convinced the other person is the problem.
That is why Paul’s warning in 1 Corinthians 7 is so sobering.
He understands that sexual intimacy is not spiritually irrelevant.
Yet Paul’s answer is never coercion.
And underneath it all is something even greater:
Because maybe the real question is not merely whether you withheld sex last night.
Maybe the deeper question is what you do when someone you vowed to love disappoints you.
Do you withdraw love until they perform correctly?
there is another marriage Scripture wants you to see.
And this is where the story becomes almost unbearable.
Because Jesus knew exactly what kind of Bride He was pursuing.
Not spotless because she had never sinned.
Not faithful because she had never wandered.
Not beautiful because she had never been stained.
People who promised God, “Never again,” and returned to the same darkness.
People who sang worship songs on Sunday and entertained temptation on Monday.
People who knew Bible verses but still knew exactly how to wound their spouse.
People who demanded grace from God while rationing grace at home.
The Gospel is not God shrugging at betrayal.
The Gospel is God dealing with sin so completely that the Son of God bears judgment at the cross and sinners who repent and believe can be forgiven, cleansed, reconciled, and made new.
Jesus did not come merely to make bad marriages slightly more tolerable.
He came to resurrect dead hearts.
And sometimes the first corpse He confronts is our pride.
Maybe you came into this article wanting ammunition.
You wanted a verse proving your spouse wrong.
Instead, Scripture turned the weapon around and became a mirror.
perhaps your wife does not need another lecture about submission.
Perhaps she needs to see what sacrificial love looks like when it has your face.
perhaps your husband does not need another calculated night of rejection designed to make him hurt.
“I want us healed, but I cannot keep pretending everything is okay.”
And husband, if your wife tells you intimacy has become painful, frightening, emotionally unsafe, pressured, or disconnected from how you treat her outside the bedroom...
Do not reach for a proof text before reaching for humility.

If your spouse has experienced sexual trauma, abuse, or coercion, healing may require time, wisdom, patience, pastoral care, and appropriately qualified professional support. “Do not deprive one another” is not a divine command to retraumatize someone.
Jesus is not glorified when Scripture is used to silence suffering.
Neither is He glorified when suffering becomes permission to cultivate revenge.
Both roads must eventually come to the cross.
There, repentance becomes more than saying, “Sorry you were offended.”
“I wanted you to hurt because I was hurting.”
That may be one of the holiest sentences ever spoken in a bedroom.
Not because the bedroom itself saves anyone.
But redeemed people learn to repent.
And repentance can change the atmosphere of a home.
Maybe tonight does not need to end in sex.
Maybe tonight needs to end in truth.
Maybe you need to sit beside your spouse and finally say what both of you have been avoiding.
Maybe you need to confess pornography.
Maybe you need to confess cruelty.
Maybe you need to confess emotional neglect.
Maybe you need to confess manipulation.
Maybe you need to confess that physical intimacy has become something you demand rather than something you lovingly share.
Maybe you need to confess that you have been withholding affection specifically to punish.
Maybe there are wounds far beyond what one article can address.
But somewhere healing has to begin.
Because Jesus may show you things about yourself you were hoping this article would say about your spouse.
But grace is not afraid of exposure.
Grace walks into rooms shame has kept locked for years.
And when Jesus exposes sin, He does not expose it so repentant sinners can remain chained to it.
This is why our message will always be From Scandal to Grace.
The scandal may be what happened in your marriage.
But scandal does not have to write the final chapter.
Jesus still restores what pride has shattered.
Jesus still teaches selfish people how to love.
Jesus still teaches wounded people how to forgive wisely.
Jesus still teaches married people that covenant is not a license to possess another person...
but a holy place to practice sacrificial love.
So, can you withhold sex to punish your spouse?

If by “withhold” we mean deliberately using sexual rejection as retaliation, leverage, manipulation, humiliation, or punishment, Scripture gives us no permission to turn marital intimacy into a weapon.
But Scripture gives equally no permission to coerce a spouse into sex.
It is meant to exist inside covenant faithfulness, mutuality, honor, understanding, self-giving love, and concern for one another.
Sometimes legitimate circumstances require saying not tonight.
Sometimes love says, “Something between us is wounded and we need to talk.”
and that is exactly why I am doing it.”
And perhaps you recognized yourself somewhere in these words.
If you have been punishing your spouse, repent.
If you have been pressuring your spouse, repent.
If you have been selfish, repent.
If you have weaponized Scripture, repent.
If you have been nursing resentment while pretending everything is fine, bring it before Christ.

And if your spouse has genuinely harmed you, forgiveness does not require pretending the harm never happened, abandoning wise boundaries, or remaining silently in danger. Seek trustworthy help where necessary. Biblical reconciliation is built on truth, repentance, wisdom, and grace—not denial.
Not because strangers need the details of your marriage.
Some things belong in private conversations, pastoral care, counseling rooms, and prayer.
But there is something powerful about refusing to pretend you have nothing left to surrender.
Not to send a passive-aggressive message to your spouse.
Please do not weaponize this article either.
We glorify God through lives surrendered to Christ.
But one practical way you can help Gospel-centered resources reach more people is to support the ministry that produces and distributes them.
Invite the believer whose marriage is struggling.
Invite the Christian who has grown cold.
Invite even the person who does not yet believe.
Not because Gospel Warrior is the answer.
Our job is simply to keep pointing people toward Him.
Because someday the most important victory in your marriage may not be the night your spouse finally admitted you were right.
It may be the night both of you stopped trying to punish each other...
and asked Him to teach you how to love again.
Never use the vulnerability of the person you vowed to love as the place where you choose to make them bleed.
